title: a canon write reports ok, lands in the store, and intentd's disk ingest reverts it -- the LAST write of a batch
body:
**A CANON WRITE REPORTS `ok: ... created` AND IS SILENTLY LOST WHEN IT FOLLOWS TWO OTHERS IN QUICK SUCCESSION.**

**TWO INDEPENDENT INSTANCES, TWO DIFFERENT VERBS, SAME POSITION.** vc lost `AC-17.17` as the third of three rapid `ac new` calls in one shell invocation; ic lost `AT-00.7` as the third of three rapid `at new` calls in one shell invocation. Both printed `ok: ... created`. Both were absent afterwards from the extract, from `acceptance.md`, and from `ac list` / `at list`. **Both landed and verified when the identical call was re-run alone minutes later.**

The loss is silent in the worst direction: the verb's own success line is the only report, and it is wrong. **A commit message then carries the belief forward** -- `222e5d57` says *mint AC-17.15/16/17* and has never contained 17.17 -- so three boards believed a row existed.

**HYPOTHESIS, MECHANISM-LEVEL, NOT YET DRIVEN TO A DELIBERATE REPRODUCTION.** `ac new` / `at new` write the store and re-render `acceptance.md`. `intentd` registers a project and watches it -- `registry.rs`: *a project the daemon is answering for is a project the daemon is watching*, and the watch wraps a **debouncer**. The watcher treats the render as an external edit and ingests it back into the store. On rapid successive calls the debounced ingest of render N can land after write N+1, overwriting it. A debouncer collapsing three rapid renders into one late ingest is exactly the shape that loses the last write and no other.

**EVIDENCE FOR, AND ITS LIMIT STATED.** In a freshly created scratch project outside the live tree, **18 rapid `ac new` calls across six trials of three lost nothing** -- 3 of 3 every time. The two real losses are both in this project, which the daemon has served all day and therefore watches. **WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: that the scratch project was unregistered.** `daemon status` answers from both locations and does not itself register anything, and the calls in both trees ran in-process rather than through `--daemon`, so the in-process path is not the discriminator. The registration state of the scratch tree was not measured, so the two arms differ in a way that is strongly suggested and not isolated.

**WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT:** drive three rapid writes against a project whose registration state is known in both directions, and read the daemon's ingest counter (`registry.rs` exposes `ingested()`) either side of the burst.

**MITIGATION IN USE NOW, AND IT IS NOT A FIX:** one canon write at a time, then verify the artefact -- the extract and the rendered doc -- never the tool's `ok` line. Both nodes adopted it after their own instance. **A discipline is the wrong shape of answer for a write that reports success and does not happen.**


---

## DRIVEN 2026-09-02 21:40Z (vc): THE HYPOTHESIS ABOVE IS CONFIRMED BY THE EVENT LOG, AND ONE DETAIL OF THIS FILING IS WRONG

**THE INGEST IS NOT AN INFERENCE ANY MORE -- IT IS AN EVENT, INTERLEAVED, WITH A DIFFERENT PRINCIPAL.** `event_log` in `intent/.cache/intent.db` records both episodes, and both have the same signature:

```
21:34:14.230  ac.put               ST0065/AC-00.8   local
21:34:14.555  at.put               ST0065/AT-00.8   local     <- the write that vanished
21:34:15.623  disk.sync_from_disk  <project uuid>   intentd   <- +1.068s, DIFFERENT ACTOR
21:34:50.929  at.put               ST0065/AT-00.8   local     <- retry, no ingest racing it

19:12:20.102  at.put               ST0065/AT-00.6   local
19:12:20.575  at.put               ST0065/AT-00.7   local     <- the write that vanished
19:12:21.616  disk.sync_from_disk  <project uuid>   intentd   <- +1.041s
19:12:46.366  at.put               ST0065/AT-00.7   local     <- retry
```

**THE LOST WRITE REACHED THE STORE.** Its `at.put` is logged in both episodes. So this was never a write that failed to happen -- it happened, was recorded, and was subsequently REVERTED by `intentd`'s `disk.sync_from_disk`. That is why the `ok` line was honest and the row was still gone: **two actors, and the second one wins.**

**THE +1.05s GAP IS THE DEBOUNCE THIS FILING PREDICTED** (1.068s and 1.041s, two samples). The daemon was live throughout -- `pgrep` shows `/Users/matts/.local/bin/intentd`.

**AND A SECOND WRITE TO THE SAME ID PROVES THE ROW WAS ABSENT, WITHOUT NEEDING A READ AT ALL.** Driven the same session: `at new` and `ac new` BOTH refuse a taken id (`ST0065 already has acceptance test AT-00.8, and a create must not replace it` -- and the refusal states nothing was written). **So a second `at.put` that SUCCEEDS on an id is proof that id was free at that moment.** This retires the store-versus-projection ambiguity that would otherwise have sat under every read-back here: `at list`, the canon extract and `at edit` could all in principle have been reading the projection, but a successful create cannot be explained by a stale projection.

**THE TITLE AND THE FRAMING ARE WRONG ON ONE POINT: IT IS THE LAST WRITE OF A BATCH, NOT THE THIRD.** At N=3 the third and the last are the same row, so the two episodes never discriminated them. **cc identified this a priori, before this evidence existed**, on the ground that a process exiting before its write settles puts exactly the final one at risk and needs no positional mechanism. The event log agrees: the ingest lands after the LAST write, and what it reverts is whatever the last write did. **Any reproduction must therefore use N != 3.**

**WHAT THIS STILL DOES NOT ESTABLISH.** Causation is supported by two coincidences with a consistent gap; it is not proven. The ingest is the only intervening event in both windows, which is strong, but no arm here suppressed the ingest and observed the loss disappear. **Two cheap discriminators, in order of cost:** space the writes past the debounce (>2s apart) and see whether the loss goes away, which needs nothing from anybody; or drive a burst with the daemon stopped, which is an hv window and NOT a node's to take (`0196`) -- **and it is the same window `ST0057 AT-07.5` already needs, so the two collapse into one sitting.**

**THE MITIGATION IS UNCHANGED AND STILL NOT A FIX**, but its reason is now sharper: verifying the artefact after the write is not protection against a slow ingest, because the ingest can land after the verification too. **The real cure is on the daemon side -- an ingest must not revert store state newer than the disk it read.**

**CORRECTION, SAME SESSION, TO THE LINE DIRECTLY ABOVE: THE DEBOUNCE IS 250ms, NOT ~1s.** `native/rust/crates/intentd/src/watch.rs:51` -- `const QUIET: Duration = Duration::from_millis(250)`, passed to `new_debouncer` at `:92`. **Calling the observed 1.05s gap "the debounce" was reading a constant off a measurement instead of off the source, which is this estate's own staleness class pointed at a number.**

**THE MECHANISM IS SHARPER WITH THE REAL VALUE, NOT WEAKER.** A debouncer restarts its quiet period on every event, so a burst of rapid writes keeps resetting it and the ingest fires 250ms after the **LAST** write of the burst. **That is a mechanistic derivation of why the final write is the exposed one, rather than an inference from two samples.**

**WHAT IS NOW UNEXPLAINED AND IS STATED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED OVER: the gap from last write to the logged `disk.sync_from_disk` is ~1.05s, and 250ms of it is the quiet period.** The remaining ~800ms is most plausibly the ingest's own duration with the event logged on completion -- **but that is a guess about when the row is written, and it has not been checked.** It matters for the drive: if the event is logged at completion, the revert may land materially later than 250ms after the burst, so a read-back that verifies too promptly can still see a row that is about to be reverted.

---

## CENSUS OF WHAT IS ALREADY LOST, 2026-09-02 21:45Z (vc, on cc's design). ONE LIVE LOSS FOUND AND REPAIRED

**cc's point, and it outranked the drive: nobody had asked how much is already gone.** If a live `intentd` reverts the last write of a burst then this has been true for every node writing canon all day, every day, and **the class is silent by construction** -- the two known episodes were caught by luck.

**POPULATION.** `event_log`, 1287 events, 2026-08-18T09:21Z to 2026-09-02T21:44Z: 988 writes, 299 `disk.sync_from_disk`. **AT RISK = the write immediately preceding an ingest, within 2s: FIFTEEN.**

**THE 2s WINDOW IS AN EMPIRICAL CHOICE FROM TWO SAMPLES AND IS NOT DERIVED.** The quiet period is 250ms; the observed last-write-to-logged-ingest is ~1.05s; the ~800ms between is unexplained. **So the at-risk figure is a threshold decision, and a bound that looks computed while being guessed is worse than none.** All fifteen observed gaps fall in 0.775s-1.559s, so the set is insensitive to the threshold anywhere between 1.6s and 2s -- but that is a property of this sample, not a derivation.

**THE CENSUS DID NOT STAY A BOUND, BECAUSE THE PAYLOADS RECORD INTENT.** Each event carries what the write meant to do (`{"from":"open","to":"closed"}`, a target status, a byte count, a title), so every at-risk write is individually checkable against current state. **The population is RESOLVED rather than bracketed:**

- **ONE LOSS STILL LIVE, NOW REPAIRED: issue `0202`.** Three writes in 1.1s -- body edit, title edit to *NOT A DEFECT: the scaffolding test invokes the pruned v2 `intent_claude_upgrade`*, then `issues.close` -- ingest +1.164s after the close. **Status was `open` with an empty `closed` column 37 hours later, and `issues.open` has NEVER occurred in the entire log (count 0), so a legitimate reopen is excluded rather than assumed.** A triaged not-a-defect sat in the open list because its close was reverted. Re-closed 2026-09-02T21:46:53Z and verified past the window.
- **FIVE LOST AND REPAIRED BY HAND AT THE TIME:** `ST0057/AC-12.2`, `ST0056/AC-17.17`, `ST0065/AT-00.7`, `ST0065/AT-00.8` -- each proven by a second SUCCESSFUL `.put` on the same id, which given the create-refuses-a-taken-id semantics proves the row was absent. **`ST0064/AC-01.5` is a fifth, evidenced differently: its stored evidence text diverges from the payload by two words (`Grammar:` against `Grammar confirmed:`), so it was retyped rather than restored.**
- **THE REMAINING NINE ARE VERIFIED IN THEIR INTENDED STATE** -- `ST0057` WP13 exists with its title and scope; `AT-07.5`, `AT-07.6`, `AT-00.13`, `AT-08.4`, `AT-00.3` all green as the payloads intended; the `ac-06_1-unstable-causes.md` attachment present; issue `0200`'s body exactly the intended 4406 bytes.

**A CORRECTION TO THIS CENSUS'S OWN FIRST CUT.** The first lower bound counted *any later write to the same subject* as a confirmed loss and returned 8. **That is not a retry signature** -- a legitimate edit twenty minutes later proves nothing, and three of the eight had gaps of 457s, 984s and 1237s. **Only a second successful `.put` proves absence**, because only creates refuse a taken id; `set`, `edit` and `satisfy` are all writable over a row that already exists. The rigorous count is above.

**WHAT THIS CENSUS CANNOT SEE, AND IT IS THE HALF THAT MATTERS.** It finds losses whose write is adjacent to a logged ingest. **A loss whose repair happened silently, or whose intent was never re-attempted and never noticed, is invisible to the retry arm by construction.** And **"the ingest is the only intervening event" is a statement about the LOG, not about the machine** -- anything the log does not record would not appear there either way.

**THE PROVENANCE COROLLARY, PROMOTED OUT OF AN ASIDE:** all eight `ST0065` test rows carry an identical `written_at` to the millisecond, later than every write that made them, because the ingest rewrites rows wholesale. **No row-level timestamp in this store is provenance for anything. `event_log` is the only provenance surface in the system**, which is also why this census was possible at all.

**AND THE FORK THE LOG CANNOT RESOLVE (cc).** At the moment of the ingest, did the DISK file contain the lost row? **If disk was missing it, this is a store-commit / disk-flush ordering race, the debounce interval is incidental, and tuning it treats a symptom.** If disk had it and the ingest reverted anyway, the ingest is wrong and the flush is innocent. **Two defects, two different fixes, and the event log records that the ingest ran, not what it read.** Capturing the file's content or mtime at ingest time is what separates them, and it belongs ahead of any spacing arm.
